categories.description: Cheat sheet for sound system architecture in Linux

content.title: Sound Flow: From Binary Stream to Sound
content.description: How sound data flows from the application to actual sound in speakers.
tips: Sound is represented as a binary stream of digital data (0s and 1s) which is converted into sound waves by the sound card.
Digital data is buffered and processed in chunks before being played.

content.title: What is ALSA?
content.description: ALSA provides kernel-level drivers and a user-space library for low-level communication with the sound card.
tips: ALSA handles the core communication between the operating system and the sound card.
Applications can talk directly to ALSA for basic sound functionality, but more complex setups often use PulseAudio or PipeWire.

content.title: What is PulseAudio?
content.description: PulseAudio is a sound server that sits between ALSA and applications, offering advanced features like sound mixing and per-application volume control.
tips: PulseAudio allows multiple programs to play sound at the same time and control volumes independently.
It also manages audio devices like headphones, speakers, and Bluetooth connections.

content.title: What is PipeWire?
content.description: PipeWire is a modern alternative to PulseAudio, designed to handle both audio and video streams with better performance and lower latency.
tips: PipeWire is designed for both audio and video streams, making it more future-proof for multimedia systems.
It can replace both PulseAudio and JACK for professional audio use.

topics.title: Using systemctl to Manage Sound Services

content.title: Managing Sound Services with systemctl
content.description: How to use systemctl to manage PulseAudio and PipeWire services on Linux.
tips: Use systemctl with the --user flag to manage sound services that run per user.
PipeWire can be used as a drop-in replacement for PulseAudio, and systemctl can be used to switch between them.
